blocks.content: Most failures in distributed systems are temporary. A payment gateway times out not because the gateway is broken but because it was briefly overloaded.

A database connection drops not because the database is down but because a network hiccup lasted 200ms. Retrying those calls at the right time, with the right limits recovers from failures that would otherwise reach the user as errors.
This lesson covers: fixed delay, exponential backoff, jitter, retry predicates, idempotency, max attempts, dead-letter fallback, and the mistakes that turn a retry mechanism into an outage amplifier.
1. What is Retryable?
A retry mechanism in Low-Level Design (LLD) is a fault-tolerance technique that automatically re-executes an operation when it fails due to a temporary or transient issue.
Instead of immediately treating the failure as permanent, the system attempts the operation again based on a predefined retry policy.
The goal is to improve reliability and availability by handling short-lived failures such as network timeouts, temporary service outages, or intermittent communication errors.
A retry mechanism typically defines how many times an operation should be retried, how long the system should wait between attempts, and which types of errors are eligible for retry.
More advanced implementations may use strategies such as exponential backoff and jitter to reduce system load and prevent large numbers of clients from retrying simultaneously.

For example, if a service request to an external API fails because of a timeout, the system may wait for a short period and retry the request. If the API becomes available during a subsequent attempt, the operation succeeds without requiring user intervention.
If all retry attempts fail, the system reports the operation as unsuccessful and may trigger additional error-handling mechanisms.

blocks.content: 2. What makes a failure retryable?
Before writing a single retry loop, answer one question: is this failure transient? Transient failures are caused by temporary conditions network blips, overloaded upstreams, brief lock contention.

Permanent failures are caused by logic errors invalid input, missing records, authentication failures. Retrying a permanent failure wastes time and makes the error message arrive later than it should.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/1781598240824-560502356.png
Strategy 1: fixed delay retry
The simplest retry strategy: wait a fixed amount of time between each attempt. Easy to reason about, easy to implement.
The right choice when you know roughly how long the upstream needs to recover, and when the volume of retries is low enough that a stampede is not a concern.
Strategy 2: exponential backoff

Instead of waiting the same amount each time, the delay doubles on every attempt. This gives the upstream increasingly more time to recover, and dramatically reduces the load a fleet of clients puts on an already-struggling server early retries are cheap, later ones are rare.
The formula: delay = baseDelay × 2^attempt. A base of 200ms with three retries gives waits of 200ms, 400ms, 800ms. A cap prevents the delay from growing unboundedly.
Strategy 3: exponential backoff with jitter
Exponential backoff is almost but not quite enough. If hundreds of clients all fail at the same moment and all back off by the same computed delay, they all retry at the same moment too.
This "thundering herd" hits the recovering server with a spike that causes it to fail again. Jitter adds randomness to the delay, spreading retries across a time window instead of synchronising them.
The standard formula: delay = random(0, min(cap, base × 2^attempt)). Full jitter is the most effective approach for reducing server load during recovery.
3. Idempotency:  the prerequisite for safe retries
A retry sends the same request more than once. If the first attempt partially succeeded before failing a payment was charged but the response never arrived a naive retry charges the user twice.
Retrying is only safe when the operation is idempotent: calling it multiple times with the same inputs produces exactly the same outcome as calling it once.
4. Dead-letter fallback
When all retry attempts are exhausted, the failure is no longer transient or at least it has exceeded what the system is willing to wait for.
The response at this point is to route the failed operation to a dead-letter queue or a fallback handler, rather than silently dropping it or crashing.
Dead-lettered operations can be replayed manually, alerted on, or used to trigger circuit breakers.

blocks.content: 5. Design rules

["Always define a retry predicate. Never catchExceptionbroadly and retry everything. Explicitly enumerate which exception types are transient. Permanent failures should propagate immediately.
","Always set a max attempts cap. An uncapped retry loop can run forever under certain failure modes, holding threads or coroutines hostage. Three to five attempts covers the vast majority of transient failures.
","Use jitter in high-concurrency systems. Fixed and pure exponential backoff cause synchronized retry storms when many clients fail together. Add randomness proportional to the computed ceiling.
","Verify idempotency before retrying writes. Reads are safe to retry unconditionally. Writes need either server-side idempotency keys or idempotent operation semantics (e.g. PUT instead of POST).
","Never retry inside a database transaction. A transaction that retries an inner call holds locks for the full retry duration, causing cascading lock contention. Retry at the level above the transaction boundary.
","Never swallow the final exception. When retries are exhausted, the exception must go somewhere a DLQ, an alert, a logged error. Catching and returning null silently hides failures that need human attention.
","Respect Retry-After headers. When an upstream returns HTTP 429 with aRetry-Afterheader, use that value as the delay instead of your computed backoff. Ignoring it makes you an abusive client.
"]
items: Always define a retry predicate. Never catchExceptionbroadly and retry everything. Explicitly enumerate which exception types are transient. Permanent failures should propagate immediately.

Always set a max attempts cap. An uncapped retry loop can run forever under certain failure modes, holding threads or coroutines hostage. Three to five attempts covers the vast majority of transient failures.
Use jitter in high-concurrency systems. Fixed and pure exponential backoff cause synchronized retry storms when many clients fail together. Add randomness proportional to the computed ceiling.
Verify idempotency before retrying writes. Reads are safe to retry unconditionally. Writes need either server-side idempotency keys or idempotent operation semantics (e.g. PUT instead of POST).

Never retry inside a database transaction. A transaction that retries an inner call holds locks for the full retry duration, causing cascading lock contention. Retry at the level above the transaction boundary.

Never swallow the final exception. When retries are exhausted, the exception must go somewhere a DLQ, an alert, a logged error. Catching and returning null silently hides failures that need human attention.
Respect Retry-After headers. When an upstream returns HTTP 429 with aRetry-Afterheader, use that value as the delay instead of your computed backoff. Ignoring it makes you an abusive client.

blocks.content: 6. Common mistakes
Mistake 1: retrying 400 Bad Request

A 400 means the server understood the request and rejected it because the input was wrong. Retrying the identical request produces the identical rejection, forever. Always check the status code or exception type before deciding to retry.
Mistake 2: no jitter in a fleet

Thirty services all time out at second 5.000 and all retry at second 5.500. The overloaded server gets hit with thirty simultaneous retries a thundering herd. Jitter is not optional in any system where multiple clients can fail at the same time.
Mistake 3: retrying inside a transaction

The transaction holds a row-level lock from attempt 1. Attempt 2 waits behind a fresh connection. Attempt 3 makes it three waiters. By the time any of them succeed the transaction timeout has fired. Retry at the service layer, not inside the repository layer.
Mistake 4: generating a new idempotency key per retry

The whole point of the key is that it is stable across attempts. Generating a new UUID on each retry sends three separate payments and charges the user three times. Generate the key once, before the first attempt, and pass it through every retry.
Mistake 5: no cap on exponential delay
Without a cap, attempt 20 of an exponential backoff with base 200ms computes a delay of 200ms × 2²⁰ = 209 seconds.
The operation is effectively dead at that point but the retry loop keeps running. Always set a sensible cap typically 10–30 seconds for interactive flows, up to a few minutes for background jobs.
7. Quick reference

["Fixed delay Same wait every time. Simple, predictable. Right for low-volume flows with known recovery time.
","Exponential backoff Delay doubles each attempt. Reduces load on struggling upstream. Always set a cap.
","Jitter Randomises the delay within the computed ceiling. Prevents thundering herds in concurrent systems.
","Retry predicate The explicit list of exception types or status codes that are safe to retry. Everything else fails immediately.
","Idempotency key A stable token generated before the first attempt and reused on every retry. Prevents duplicate side effects.
","Dead-letter queue Where operations go when all retries are exhausted. Enables manual replay, alerting, and circuit breaking."]
items: Fixed delay Same wait every time. Simple, predictable. Right for low-volume flows with known recovery time.
Exponential backoff Delay doubles each attempt. Reduces load on struggling upstream. Always set a cap.
Jitter Randomises the delay within the computed ceiling. Prevents thundering herds in concurrent systems.
Retry predicate The explicit list of exception types or status codes that are safe to retry. Everything else fails immediately.
Idempotency key A stable token generated before the first attempt and reused on every retry. Prevents duplicate side effects.
Dead-letter queue Where operations go when all retries are exhausted. Enables manual replay, alerting, and circuit breaking.
